screeningScope: Full-text source, eligibility, study-design, taxonomy, and synthesis-readiness review of queue positions 1-12 after Batch 09 publication.

decisionDefinitions.INCLUDE: Eligible for evidence extraction and synthesis after full-text review.
decisionDefinitions.DEGRADED: A required source or verification element was unavailable.

records.sourceFile: Examination of the Impact of Substance Use on Sport Training and Competition in Collegiate Athletes.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: A four-item self-report measure of how alcohol and illicit-drug use interferes with sport training and competition was evaluated in 285 collegiate athletes. One-week test-retest reliability was good, scores related positively to psychiatric symptoms, substance-use frequency, and age, and males scored higher. In a selected 74-athlete subsample, the difference between athletes with and without a current substance-use disorder was only a nonsignificant trend.
records.limitations: The study validates a brief self-report construct rather than diagnosing substance-use disorder or predicting objective sport outcomes. Disclosure may be affected by stigma and consequences, and the diagnostic comparison used a small, intervention-interested substance-using subsample with a nonsignificant p value of 0.08.
records.synthesisCaution: Use the items to support confidential conversation and referral within an established clinical pathway. Do not interpret a score as a diagnosis, a causal measure of performance loss, or a disciplinary trigger.

records.sourceFile: On the value of a premium college football player - Evaluating the literature.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: This sports-economics article reviewed historical approaches to estimating the marginal revenue product of premium college football players and updated estimates using contemporary revenue and player data. Across methods, top players appeared to generate substantially more institutional value than cost-of-attendance compensation, while the precise magnitude of that gap remained uncertain.
records.limitations: Marginal revenue product depends heavily on model specification, revenue allocation, the definition of a premium player, and assumptions about causality. School fixed effects can absorb stable program advantages, player talent is endogenous to program context, and the legal and compensation environment has continued to change.
records.synthesisCaution: Treat the paper as institutional and athlete-welfare context, not evidence about health, training, selection, or an individual athlete's market value. Its estimates should not be used for player-level compensation decisions without current legal and economic analysis.

records.sourceFile: Injury prevention in professional soccer players - Can re-warmup training be organized in the post-warmup and half-time during a soccer game in a short time.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: This narrative review screened literature on brief re-warm-ups that could fit the post-warm-up delay or halftime in professional soccer and included 26 papers aligned with its objectives. It highlighted one protocol of one minute at approximately 90% VO2max that preserved sprint and strength performance and muscle temperature after passive rest without added perceived or physiological fatigue.
records.limitations: The review used a narrative synthesis, did not provide a systematic certainty assessment, and drew its one-minute recommendation primarily from a limited evidence base. Much of the evidence concerned performance and temperature rather than observed injury incidence, and practical constraints vary across teams and competitions.
records.synthesisCaution: A brief high-intensity re-warm-up is a promising operational template, not a proven injury-prevention intervention or universal one-minute prescription. Test the activity, timing, space, and individual tolerance in the team's actual match workflow.

records.sourceFile: Muscle activity asymmetry of the lower limbs during sprinting in elite soccer players.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Sixteen elite male soccer players completed two maximal 30-m sprints while bilateral textile EMG recorded quadriceps, hamstring, and gluteal activity. Regression analyses linked side-to-side hamstring and gluteal activity asymmetry with 5-m and 30-m sprint times, and descriptive comparisons showed the greatest imbalance in the gluteal muscles and the smallest in the quadriceps.
records.limitations: The small cross-sectional laboratory sample cannot determine whether EMG asymmetry caused slower sprinting or injury. Textile EMG represents broad muscle-group activation, external sprint mechanics and lower-leg muscles were not evaluated, and the reported associations were not prospectively validated.
records.synthesisCaution: Use bilateral EMG as one descriptive view of sprint strategy. Do not label an athlete injured or prescribe corrective work from a single asymmetry value, and do not infer that targeted gluteal or hamstring activation will prevent injury.

records.sourceFile: Peak instantaneous PlayerLoad metrics highlight movement strategy deficits in professional male soccer players.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Twenty-five professional male soccer players completed anterior, medial, and lateral single-leg hops with a mid-calf accelerometer. Twelve had no previous injury and 13 had a previous injury. Previously injured players hopped less far, and their affected limb took longer to reach peak mediolateral loading, although peak loading was not consistently lower and no overall bilateral asymmetry was detected.
records.limitations: This was a one-session study from one English Championship club with a small mixed-injury sample and retrospective injury histories. Accelerometer-derived PlayerLoad is a device-specific surrogate, and the study did not establish prospective injury risk, readiness thresholds, or responsiveness to rehabilitation.
records.synthesisCaution: Pair movement-strategy metrics with task performance and both-limb assessment, but do not use peak PlayerLoad or time-to-peak alone for injury prediction or return-to-sport clearance.

records.sourceFile: Performance of Future Elite Players at The NFL Combine.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Secondary data from 5,506 athletes who attended the NFL Scouting Combine and were drafted from 2002 through 2016 linked seven anthropometric and physical-test measures with later Pro Bowl and All-Pro recognition. Mean differences varied by position, with faster 40-yard times and selected jump, bench, shuttle, or three-cone characteristics appearing in different elite-award groups.
records.limitations: The retrospective data excluded undrafted attendees and players who did not attend the combine, contained missing tests, and included athletes whose careers were still active. Awards are partly voting-based and confounded by opportunity, role, team context, and football skill; multiple position-level comparisons do not create a validated prediction model.
records.synthesisCaution: Use combine distributions as position-specific descriptive context and goal-setting inputs. Do not treat a single test, profile, or award association as proof of future NFL success or as a reason to force body-mass change.

records.sourceFile: Effects of chronic static stretching interventions on jumping and sprinting performance - A systematic review with multilevel meta-analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Fourteen chronic static-stretching studies contributed 29 effects: 20 jumping and nine sprinting. The multilevel meta-analysis found a statistically significant but trivial improvement in jumping (effect size 0.16, p=0.04), no significant jump subgroup effects, and no significant sprint effect (p=0.08), despite positive individual tests in parts of the literature.
records.limitations: The small evidence base varied in stretching dose, intensity, population, comparator, and performance test. Positive study-level results did not translate into consistent pooled or subgroup effects, and the review could not determine whether higher-volume or higher-intensity stretching would produce meaningful sport performance gains.
records.synthesisCaution: Use chronic static stretching when range-of-motion goals or athlete preference justify it, not as a primary sprint or jump development method. Preserve specific sprint, plyometric, and resistance training for performance adaptation.

records.sourceFile: Effects of combined uphill-downhill sprinting vs resisted sprinting methods on sprint performance - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Twenty-two studies yielded 24 intervention groups with at least four weeks of training: six combined uphill-downhill and 18 resisted-sprint groups, each compared with traditional sprinting. Uphill-downhill training had a small advantage over traditional sprinting (SMD -0.41, 95% CI -0.79 to -0.03), while resisted sprinting did not (SMD -0.14, 95% CI -0.36 to 0.07).
records.limitations: Only six uphill-downhill groups were available, five were nonprofessional, and none tested distances below 35 m, so early-acceleration effects cannot be inferred. Populations, slopes, resistance methods, loads, and outcomes varied, and limited group counts constrained subgroup and meta-regression analyses.
records.synthesisCaution: The small pooled advantage makes combined hill work a plausible option, not proof that it is universally superior. Hill geometry cannot be adjusted like a sled load, and the protocol should be selected around surface safety, sprint phase, athlete skill, and measured response.

records.sourceFile: Effects of Post-Exercise Heat Exposure on Acute Recovery and Training-Induced Performance Adaptations - A Systematic Review.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Fourteen randomized or crossover studies involving 194 healthy adults evaluated sauna, hot-water immersion, or other whole-body heat exposure after exercise. Among nine acute studies, four found no performance-recovery effect, four a benefit, and one an adverse effect. Five longer interventions suggested possible running benefit in heat but no cycling or VO2max benefit.
records.limitations: Evidence quality was low to moderate, participant samples were small, and heat mode, temperature, dose, training, outcome, and recovery interval were too heterogeneous for meta-analysis. The mixed acute findings and sport-specific chronic results prevent a general conclusion about recovery or adaptation.
records.synthesisCaution: Heat is an added physiological load, not a universally restorative modality. Define whether the goal is heat acclimation, recovery, or adaptation; control hydration and medical risk; and monitor individual response before routine use.

records.sourceFile: Effects of Resisted-Sprint Training on Sprint Performance and Mechanics - A Systematic Review and Meta-AnalysisFocusing on Load Magnitude.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Forty-nine resisted-sprint studies with 1,281 participants were synthesized using direct, multilevel, and network models. Resisted sprinting modestly outperformed unresisted sprinting overall (Hedges' g -0.30; moderate certainty), with advantages detected for moderate and very heavy loads but not light or heavy categories. Benefits were concentrated in early acceleration, especially 0-5 m.
records.limitations: All randomized studies were rated high risk of bias and many nonrandomized studies had serious risk. Female representation was low, load categories were uneven, mechanical outcomes were sparse, and the reported 20.7% body-mass meta-regression threshold is data-dependent rather than a validated prescription boundary.
records.synthesisCaution: Choose resistance from the intended sprint phase, actual velocity decrement, mechanics, volume, and athlete training status. Do not convert the pooled threshold or load labels into a universal sled prescription, and retain unresisted sprint exposure.

records.sourceFile: Effects of sleep deprivation on sports performance and perceived exertion in athletes and non-athletes -A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Forty-five randomized or randomized-crossover studies showed that sleep deprivation impaired athlete aerobic endurance (SMD -0.66), explosive power (-0.63), maximum force (-0.35), speed (-0.52), and skill control (-0.87), while increasing perceived exertion (0.39). Healthy non-athletes also showed reduced aerobic endurance, and several partial-deprivation and time-of-day subgroups were adverse.
records.limitations: Sleep protocols, tests, populations, baseline sleep control, and risk of bias varied across outcomes and subgroup analyses. Female participation was too limited for sex-specific analysis, some domains contained few studies, and subgroup estimates should not be interpreted as precise timing rules.
records.synthesisCaution: Protect sleep before high-consequence training and competition and adjust expectations after verified sleep loss. Do not use pooled subgroup effects to promise a specific decrement or to infer that every athlete will respond identically.

records.sourceFile: Efficacy of heavy eccentric calf training for treating mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy- a systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Seven trials with 241 adults with chronic mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy compared heavy eccentric calf training with natural history, traditional physiotherapy, or other exercise. VISA-A favored eccentric training over natural history by 20.6 points and traditional physiotherapy by 17.7 points, while sensitivity analysis modestly favored other exercise over eccentric training by 5.65 points.
records.limitations: All trials were small and the evidence was rated low or very low quality. Participants were generally 37-49 years old with long symptom duration, intervention adherence and loading varied, publication bias could not be assessed, and the advantage of other exercise after sensitivity analysis was unlikely to be clinically important.
records.synthesisCaution: Heavy eccentric calf training is one loading option, not the required or proven best Achilles protocol. Select and progress calf loading around symptoms, capacity, adherence, sport demands, and the rest of the return-to-running plan.
